lines.text: Stone towns on the Indian Ocean, a railway into the highlands, a hard fight for freedom and the fastest runners on Earth. This is the story of Kenya.
By about the year twelve hundred, a Swahili stone town stood at Gedi on the coast. Its ruins still rise among the trees.
Up the coast, Lamu was growing too. Today it is the oldest Swahili town where people still live.
Then the Portuguese arrived by sea. In 1593 they built Fort Jesus to guard the harbour at Mombasa.
Mombasa itself was an old Swahili port, trading across the Indian Ocean for centuries, and it remains Kenya's great gateway to the sea.
Along this coast the Swahili language took shape, rich in words from Arabic. Its oldest poems date from the early seventeen hundreds, and it unites East Africa still.
Inland, at the end of the eighteen hundreds, Jomo Kenyatta was born. He would lead Kenya to independence and be its first president.
In 1899 a camp for railway workers grew up on the plains. It became Nairobi, and in time, the capital.
The railway ran from Mombasa all the way to Lake Victoria. It opened the highlands to British settlers, who took much of the best land.
In 1920 Britain made Kenya a colony, and for more than forty years it ruled from Nairobi.
In 1931 Mwai Kibaki was born. Decades later he would be Kenya's third president.
Ngugi wa Thiong'o grew up under colonial rule and became one of Africa's great writers. Jailed in 1978, he chose to write in Gikuyu instead of English.
Wangari Maathai would found the Green Belt Movement and plant millions of trees, and become the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
Raila Odinga, born in 1945, would become the great opposition leader of his generation, and for a time prime minister.
In 1952 the Mau Mau rose, mostly Kikuyu fighters demanding land and freedom. Britain answered with an emergency and detention camps.
In 1961 the Maasai Mara became a reserve, the stage of the great migration, where herds pour across the plains each year.
In December 1963 Kenya became independent, with Jomo Kenyatta at its head.
William Ruto was born three years later, in 1966. In 2022 he would win the presidency.
Kenya's runners made the world take notice. Eliud Kipchoge won two Olympic marathons, and in Vienna ran one in under two hours.
At the London Olympics, David Rudisha ran the eight hundred metres faster than anyone ever had.
In 1997 Safaricom was born. Ten years later its M-Pesa let Kenyans send money by phone, long before most of the world could.
In 1998 al-Qaeda bombed the American embassy in Nairobi, and its twin in Dar es Salaam.
After the disputed election of 2007, violence tore through the country for weeks.
Out of that crisis came a new constitution in 2010, which shared power out to the counties.
In 2013 al-Shabaab gunmen attacked the Westgate mall in Nairobi and killed sixty seven people.
In 2017 a new railway opened between Mombasa and Nairobi, following the route of the old line more than a century later.
And in 2024 young Kenyans filled the streets against new taxes, a new generation making its voice heard.
From the Swahili coast to the streets of Nairobi, Kenya's story is still being written.
